functions.description: Convert the percentage prevalence, sensitivity and specificity into probabilities in the unit interval
inputs: the prevalence of the disease in the population with unit (base rate, percentage or probability)
the sensitivity of the test, i.e. the true positive rate P(positive | disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
the specificity of the test, i.e. the true negative rate P(negative | no disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
outputs: false positive probability P(positive | no disease) as one minus specificity
probability of no disease P(not disease)

functions.description: Compute the true positive joint probability, the false positive joint probability and the total probability of a positive test from prevalence, sensitivity and false positive rate by the law of total probability.
inputs: false positive probability P(positive | no disease) as one minus specificity
probability of no disease P(not disease)
outputs: true positive joint probability P(positive and disease)
false positive joint probability P(positive and no disease)
total probability of a positive test P(positive)

functions.description: Apply Bayes theorem to divide the true positive joint probability by the total probability of a positive test to get the posterior probability of disease given a positive test
inputs: true positive joint probability P(positive and disease)
total probability of a positive test P(positive)
outputs: posterior probability of disease given a positive test P(disease | positive)

functions.description: Express a probability as a percentage by multiplying it by one hundred.
inputs: posterior probability of disease given a positive test P(disease | positive)

functions.description: Compute the probability that a person has the disease given a positive test from the prevalence, sensitivity and specificity of the test.
inputs: the prevalence of the disease in the population with unit (base rate, percentage or probability)
the sensitivity of the test, i.e. the true positive rate P(positive | disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
the specificity of the test, i.e. the true negative rate P(negative | no disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
outputs: probability of disease given a positive test as a percentage and as a probability

entry_points.text: A disease affects ●1 of a population. A test for it has ●2 sensitivity and ●3 specificity. If a randomly chosen person tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease?

params.description: the prevalence of the disease in the population with unit (base rate, percentage or probability)
params.validity_range: Must be a proportion between 0 and 100 percent (0 to 1 as a probability). Strictly between 0 and 100 percent for a non-degenerate problem: at 0 no one has the disease so the posterior is 0 and the question is trivial, at 100 everyone has it so the posterior is 1 regardless of the test. Values outside 0 to 100 percent are logically impossible. Also the value must be consistent with a population, so no negative numbers.

params.description: the sensitivity of the test, i.e. the true positive rate P(positive | disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
params.validity_range: Must be between 0 and 100 percent inclusive. A sensitivity of 0 means the test never detects the disease, so P(positive) comes only from false positives and the posterior is 0 unless the false positive mass is also 0; values above 100 percent are impossible. Sensitivity and specificity are independent of prevalence and must be treated as conditional rates.

params.description: the specificity of the test, i.e. the true negative rate P(negative | no disease), with unit (percentage or probability)
params.validity_range: Must be between 0 and 100 percent inclusive. A specificity of 100 percent means no false positives, so the posterior equals 1 whenever sensitivity is positive. A specificity of 0 means every healthy person tests positive. Values outside 0 to 100 percent are logically impossible. The false positive rate used in the calculation is one minus this value, so it lies in the same range.
